channel.title: Computer Chronicle
channel.description: A weekly early-1980s computer newspaper rebuilt from the historical record — games, software, hardware, prices, charts, and culture, one week at a time.

item.title: Week of July 11-17, 1983 — Nintendo Brings the Arcade Home With Its Family Computer
item.description: At ¥14,800, Nintendo’s red-and-white Famicom arrives with two controllers and three arcade conversions. Nintendo launched its Family Computer in Japan on July 15, placing a compact red-and-white cartridge machine on shop counters for ¥14,800. The name was quickly shortened to Famicom, and the proposition was direct: swap a cartridge and bring the speed and familiarity of the arcade into the living room. Also this week: Sega Enters the Living Room With the SG-1000 · Electronic Arts' M.U.L.E. Turns Economics Into a Multiplayer Contest · Infocom's Suspended Puts Six Robots Between the Player and Disaster.

item.title: Week of July 4-10, 1983 — Coleco’s Adam Promises a Complete Computer for Under $600
item.description: The summer CES sensation combines game compatibility, high-capacity tape, word processing and a daisy-wheel printer in one mass-market package. The most talked-about personal computer of the summer is not merely a keyboard in a box. Coleco’s Adam, the lead item in the July 3 Arcade Express after its Consumer Electronics Show debut, is being pitched as a complete household system: computer, keyboard, high-capacity tape storage, word processing, joysticks and a daisy-wheel printer for a promised price below $600. Also this week: The $600 System Becomes the New Battleground · Dragon’s Lair Turns the Arcade into a Cartoon Theater · Electronic Arts Gives Designers Star Billing.

item.title: Week of June 27-July 3, 1983 — Dragon’s Lair Brings the Cartoon Arcade
item.description: Cinematronics’ laserdisc cabinet turns Don Bluth animation into the year’s loudest coin-op, and the rest of the arcade is scrambling to keep up. Just weeks after the June Consumer Electronics Show handed the home-computer business its next big products, the arcade answered with a machine that played more like a movie than a game. Cinematronics’ Dragon’s Lair, in arcades from June 1983, drove a Pioneer laserdisc player with a joystick and a single sword button, jumping between pre-animated scenes of a knight named Dirk the Daring rescuing Princess Daphne from the dragon Singe. Also this week: Coleco Pitches Adam as the Family Computer · Atari Resets Its 8-Bit Line with the 600XL and 800XL · WarGames Makes the Modem a Summer Star · The Price War Bites the Family-Room Shelf.

item.title: Week of June 20-26, 1983 — Software's Hard Sell
item.description: A $1.5 billion industry learns packaging, promotion and hit-making. Personal-computer software is becoming a packaged-goods business. SRI International projects 1983 revenue of $1.5 billion, after $1 billion in 1982 and $600 million in 1981, and TIME counts at least 230 producers chasing annual growth near 50 percent. The machine may command the showroom, but the programs now determine what owners can actually accomplish. Also this week: Coleco's Adam Takes Aim at the Family Room · Atari Clears the Deck for Four XL Machines · Programs May Soon Travel by Telephone.

item.title: Week of June 13–19, 1983 — Software's Hard Sell Becomes a Billion-Dollar Business
item.description: Commodore readies roughly 70 titles, Lotus buys attention, and software makers learn the arts of packaging and promotion. Personal-computer software is becoming a mass-market business before shoppers’ eyes. SRI International estimates that Americans bought $1 billion worth of personal-computer programs in 1982 and forecasts $1.5 billion this year, growth fast enough to turn code once passed among hobbyists into a fiercely promoted consumer product. Also this week: Coleco's Adam Resets the Complete-Computer Price · Atari Sweeps the Deck for Four XL Machines · WarGames Turns Computer Anxiety into a Hit.

item.title: Week of June 6–12, 1983 — Coleco’s $600 Adam Steals the Summer CES
item.description: A complete computer, word processor, fast tape drive and letter-quality printer promises to turn a ColecoVision household into a home office. The busiest conversation at Chicago’s June 5–8 Consumer Electronics Show begins with an unlikely challenger. Coleco, best known for ColecoVision, has unveiled Adam: an under-$600 home-computer package built around a Z80 processor, a full-size 75-key keyboard, SmartWriter word processing, BASIC, a Digital Data Pack recorder and a daisy-wheel printer. Also this week: Atari Answers With XL Computers and a Writing System · Software Price War Breaks Out at CES · WarGames Makes the Home Modem a Movie Star.

item.title: Week of May 30–June 5, 1983 — Electronic Arts' First Five Games Reach Players
item.description: A young publisher treats programmers like recording artists—and ships a remarkably varied opening slate. SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO — Ten days before this week began, the small company called Electronic Arts made its first shipment. Its May 20 slate carried five titles—Archon: The Light and the Dark, Hard Hat Mack, M.U.L.E., Worms?, and Axis Assassin—out of a warehouse and toward computer stores. The boxes announced the company’s ambition before a disk was loaded: creators’ names appeared prominently, and the packages borrowed the scale and visual confidence of record albums. Also this week: WarGames Makes Home Computing a Summer-Movie Star · Portable and 16-Bit Machines Crowd the June BYTE · Modems Bring Computer Gamers Together.

item.title: Week of May 23–29, 1983 — Game Makers Map the Imaginative Path
item.description: Designers turn tiny memories into puzzles, adventures, and worlds the player helps complete. A May 24 New York Times personal-computing column puts game design in the spotlight. The craft is less a matter of spectacle than of carefully chosen rules, feedback, surprise, and room for the player’s imagination. Across the month’s computer magazines, the same inventive energy appears in adventure contests, modem play, construction sets, and reviews of strategy simulations—proof that the home computer is becoming a medium, not merely a machine.

item.title: Week of May 16-22, 1983 — Lode Runner gives Apple II players 150 rooms to conquer
item.description: Softalk's 1983 software record puts Doug Smith's run-climb-dig game among the year's defining Apple II releases, complete with a construction set for making new levels. Broderbund's Lode Runner turns a simple chase into a toolbox: collect the gold, outwit the guards, and then design another screen. Its mix of arcade pace and player-made levels captures the spring's most exciting computer-game idea—software that lets the owner become part designer.

item.title: Week of May 9-15, 1983 — Atari pitches a computer add-on for the VCS crowd
item.description: COMPUTE! gives May readers a close look at Atari's planned add-on computer for the 2600 game machine, a sign that console makers still want a bridge into home computing. The pitch is pure 1983 living room: keep the familiar VCS base, add a keyboard and computing capability, and turn game hardware into a starter machine. For families comparing cartridges, cassette software, and sub-$100 computer ads, the idea captures the week's uneasy overlap between console gaming and personal computing.

item.title: Week of May 2-8, 1983 — Star Wars lines up for Atari vector cabinets
item.description: Atari's Star Wars arcade machine gives the week its clearest computer-culture image: a 3-D vector trench run landing just as home computers borrow more of the arcade shelf. Trade and collector records place Atari's Star Wars arcade release in 1983, with May widely used for the cabinet's arrival. Its color-vector cockpit fantasy made a natural front-page emblem for a spring when home-computer owners were also buying arcade conversions, strategy disks, and BASIC-friendly machines from the same stores.

item.title: Week of April 25-May 1, 1983 — Arcade Alley widens the lane for computer games
item.description: Video magazine coverage treats Apple II and home-computer games as part of the same conversation as Zaxxon and Turbo. In the spring 1983 game press, the wall between coin-op excitement and personal-computer software kept getting thinner. Electronic Games expanded its Arcade Alley column to cover computer gaming, reviewing Zaxxon, Turbo, and Apple II titles in the same breath. For shoppers with an Apple II, Atari 8-bit, Commodore 64, or VIC-20, that mattered: game disks were no longer just hobby curiosities, but a front-counter reason to compare graphics, joysticks, and disk drives.

item.title: Week of April 18-24, 1983 — Pole Position keeps arcade racing in the fast lane
item.description: Atari/Namco racing cabinets remained a trade-paper and operator touchstone as home-computer aisles tried to borrow arcade excitement. By the week of April 18, arcade operators were still talking about the drawing power of Pole Position, the Namco racer Atari distributed in North America. Its sit-down cabinet, qualifying lap, and billboard-style track made it a showroom example of how arcade spectacle could sell a game before a player touched the wheel. For home-computer buyers, that arcade glow mattered: software shelves were filling with conversions and racing titles that promised a slice of the coin-op floor.

item.title: Week of April 11-17, 1983 — TI software control sparks game-counter argument
item.description: Arcade Express reported Texas Instruments wanted tighter control over TI-99/4A software, a sign that cartridge economics and home-computer publishing were colliding. The April 10 Arcade Express reached readers at the start of this Chronicle week with a sharp business-of-games lead: Texas Instruments wanted to keep control of software for the TI-99/4A. For dealers, publishers, and families watching the low-cost computer aisle, the question was not academic. A machine could be attractive on price and still be defined by who was allowed to publish for it, how cartridges reached shelves, and whether independent game makers could fill the rack quickly enough.

item.title: Week of April 4-10, 1983 — Modem games and baseball leagues reach the game rack
item.description: Computer Gaming World's May-June 1983 number put modem gaming, an adventure-games contest, and computer baseball league coverage in front of Apple II and strategy players. During the week of April 4-10, 1983, the liveliest personal-computer story was still at the game rack. Computer Gaming World Vol. 3 No. 3 carried cover lines for modem gaming, an adventure games contest, and a computer baseball league, with SSI strategy titles such as Knights of the Desert sharing space with reader-driven play. The shelf message was clear: home-computer games were becoming longer, more social, and more magazine-mediated than the arcade conversions beside them.

item.title: Week of March 21-27, 1983 — Game shelves lean into adventures and strategy
item.description: Computer Gaming World's March-April issue put Zork, Ultima II, The Cosmic Balance, and a 1983 game-industry report in front of readers as stores balanced arcade action with deeper Apple II play. During the week of March 21-27, 1983, the strongest personal-computer culture signal came from the game rack. Computer Gaming World Vol. 3 No. 2 carried a report on computer games in 1983, coverage of The Cosmic Balance, an overview of Zork, and a review of Ultima II. The mix shows why late-March shoppers saw computer games as more than arcade imitations: role-playing, text adventures, and strategy titles were becoming durable reasons to own a disk drive.

item.title: Week of March 14-20, 1983 — Home-computer readers wire up for the modem age
item.description: BYTE's March 1983 issue put a Bell 103-compatible originate/answer modem project in front of hobbyists as personal-computer communications moved from curiosity toward routine use. During the week of March 14-20, 1983, the computer press kept one eye on telecommunications. BYTE Volume 8 Number 3 listed Steve Ciarcia's Build the ECM-103, an Originate/Answer Modem, a Texas Instruments TMS99532-based Bell 103-compatible project. The article sat beside VIC-20 expansion, COMDEX impressions, storage technology, and retail advertising, a useful snapshot of how hobbyist building, home-computer upgrades, and business microcomputing shared the same magazine rack.

item.title: Week of March 7-13, 1983 — IBM puts a hard disk in the personal-computer aisle
item.description: On March 8, IBM introduced the Personal Computer XT, an expanded PC with a 10 MB fixed disk that made the office micro feel more permanent. During the week of March 7-13, 1983, IBM gave business buyers a clearer upgrade path from the original PC. Contemporary coverage described the PC XT as a new model with more expansion room and a built-in fixed disk, while the quoted $4,995 configuration kept it firmly in office-machine territory. The timing helped software such as Lotus 1-2-3 look less like an add-on and more like the daily reason to buy an IBM-compatible desk system.

item.title: Week of February 28-March 6, 1983 — Game shelves carry the home-computer pitch
item.description: As March 1983 begins, Computer Gaming World keeps strategy, adventure, and simulation titles in view while retailers use games to make home machines feel useful and fun. During the week of February 28-March 6, 1983, the home-computer market was still being explained from the shelf outward. Computer Gaming World's early-1983 issues put titles such as Serpentine, Cosmic Balance, S.E.U.I.S., Armor Assault, and wider strategy coverage in front of readers who wanted more than arcade imitation. At the same time, IBM PC shoppers were hearing the new Lotus 1-2-3 pitch, a spreadsheet/database/graphics package that had gone on sale in January and was quickly becoming a reason to take the PC seriously at work.

item.title: Week of February 21-27, 1983 — Computer games claim the brightest shelf space
item.description: As February closes, Computer Gaming World points readers toward deeper strategy and adventure titles while home-computer stores keep selling machines through games, BASIC, and office software promises. During the week of February 21-27, 1983, the home-computer story is not a single launch so much as a crowded shelf. Computer Gaming World's winter issue keeps strategy, simulation, and adventure games in front of serious players, with Serpentine, Cosmic Balance, S.E.U.I.S., Armor Assault, and other computer titles showing how far the market had moved beyond simple arcade imitation. Across the same counter, Lotus 1-2-3 was still fresh for IBM PC shoppers after its January on-sale date, while Commodore, TI, and Atari machines competed for families through memory, price, games, and programming.
